*Notes:* Under federal Standard Industrial Classification guidelines, petroleum refining (SIC 29) is classified under Division D (Manufacturing) and is thus grouped into Industrials & Manufacturing, whereas oil/gas extraction (SIC 13) and mining (SIC 10, 14) compose Energy & Mining. Software publishers and data processing services (SIC 737x) sit within Business Services (SIC 73) alongside general computer facilities, grouped here with hardware and electronics into Technology.
:::

**Statutory filings and rate limits.** Mandatory disclosures are pulled from SEC EDGAR by automated routines built on `edgartools`, covering annual reports (Form 10-K), quarterly reports (Form 10-Q), proxy statements (DEF 14A), current reports (Form 8-K) and foreign issuer annual reports (Form 20-F). The queries follow SEC fair-access rules, staying under 10 queries per second with a declared institutional user-agent header. Forms are parsed into item sections following the SEC's own item taxonomy. A 10-Q is treated as its own reporting instrument and is never pooled with a 10-K.

**Earnings call union and coverage audit.** Voluntary disclosure is followed through quarterly earnings-call transcripts taken from a deduplicated union of three providers: Hugging Face corporate earnings repositories, Equibles financial transcripts and StockAnalysis. Vendor feeds omit transcripts in ways that are not random, so every transcript is cross-verified automatically against the SEC filing dates, matching the ticker, the company name and the fiscal period marker. A firm-quarter with no vendor coverage at all (`{python} cov_call_gap_pct` of all panel firm-quarters) is marked as unmonitored (`cov_call_gap = 1`) and stored as null, not as zero. The distinction matters: otherwise an unobserved call would be analyzed as a quarter with no disclosure.

**Observation window and 2026 adjustment.** Filing and call dates run from January 1, 2021 through `{python} cov_last_date`. The 2026 observations are year-to-date up to the cut-off (`{python} cov_10k_2026` firms with Form 10-Ks, `{python} cov_10q_2026` with Form 10-Qs and `{python} cov_calls_2026` with earnings calls). For multi-year comparisons and projected annual volumes, the 2026 measures are scaled by a same-calendar-window seasonal factor (`hd_act_factor`), the ratio of full-year 2025 activity to the activity recorded in 2025 over the same calendar span.

**External patent retrieval.** As a non-textual check on technological capability, patent records published between 2021 and 2023 are retrieved from Google Patents through BigQuery. Patents are assigned to issuers in the universe using curated assignee aliases, which cover operating subsidiaries and IP holding entities, and classified with the OECD (2025) AI taxonomy: five core CPC groups taken unconditionally, plus application groups filtered on AI keywords in the title or the abstract.

@tbl-a0-derived-inventory counts, for every year of the panel, the derived artifacts the pipeline produces from the source filings and calls (analysis universe, S&P 500 as of 2021-01-01), and the number of firms with at least one such artifact.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

INV_YEARS = [2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026]
_docs = L.read_gold("document", ("covariates", "disclosure_volume"))
_docs["year"] = pd.to_datetime(_docs["fecha"]).dt.year
_docs = _docs[_docs["year"].isin(INV_YEARS)]

def _cell(n_items, n_firms):
    return f"{int(n_items):,} ({int(n_firms)})"

def _by_year(df, item_col=None, firm_col="ticker", count="rows"):
    """{year: (items, firms)} where items are rows, distinct item_col values, or a sum."""
    out = {}
    for y in INV_YEARS:
        s = df[df["year"] == y]
        if s.empty:
            out[y] = (0, 0); continue
        if count == "rows":
            items = len(s)
        elif count == "sum":
            items = s[item_col].sum()
        else:
            items = s[item_col].nunique()
        firms = s.loc[s[item_col] > 0, firm_col].nunique() if count == "sum" else s[firm_col].nunique()
        out[y] = (items, firms)
    return out
```

for ch, label in [("filing", "AI semantic frames in statutory filings"), ("call", "AI semantic frames in earnings calls")]:
    d = _by_year(_docs[_docs["channel"] == ch], item_col="n_frames", count="sum"); der_rows.append([label] + [_cell(*d[y]) for y in INV_YEARS])

_act = _act.merge(_docs[["accession_number", "year"]].drop_duplicates("accession_number"), on="accession_number", how="inner")
for ch, label in [("filing", "Disclosed AI activities in statutory filings"), ("call", "Disclosed AI activities in earnings calls")]:
    d = _by_year(_act[_act["channel"] == ch]); der_rows.append([label] + [_cell(*d[y]) for y in INV_YEARS])

Activities are counted once per firm × text × activity index and dated by the document that contains them. Post-call beta requires 63 trading days after the call, roughly one reporting quarter.

### A.2 Corpus preparation, deduplication, and prefiltering {.unnumbered}

Segmentation splits the ingested HTML and plain-text files into separate paragraph instances. Parsing drops XML tags, financial tables, ASCII graphics and exhibits that contain no prose. A text block longer than 3 characters and containing alphanumeric tokens is kept as a scorable instance.

**Cryptographic deduplication.** In statutory reporting, legal boilerplate, risk-factor language and accounting notes repeat verbatim from one quarter to the next and across exhibits. So that a duplicated paragraph neither distorts the downstream measures nor is paid for twice in LLM inference, each scorable paragraph is hashed with a 64-bit BLAKE2b hash (`text_hash`). The LLM extraction runs over unique hashes only, and the extracted frame and activity metadata are then mapped back to every document instance that shares the hash.

**Supervised GBDT prefiltering gate.** Before the language model sees anything, unique passages pass a supervised Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) classifier [@friedman2001] that removes non-AI corporate text. The model scores 39 lexical, positional and syntactic features: dense semantic anchor similarities (from `BAAI/bge-m3`), exact keyword stems, named entity frequencies and document section tags. The threshold is deliberately low ($\tau = 0.17$), which gives more than 98% recall on held-out gold annotations (Appendix B), so candidate AI disclosures survive while most of the non-technological narrative is dropped. A document with no candidate paragraph after the gate enters the panels as a true zero, not as a missing record.

```

### A.3 Structured extraction and schema taxonomies {.unnumbered}

**Extraction model selection.** The production extraction model, `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` (hosted on Amazon Bedrock in `us-east-1`, operating with zero reasoning effort), was chosen after an adversarial benchmark of seven candidate models on real 10-K disclosure excerpts (@tbl-a0-judge-selection). The comparison looked at internal field consistency, call latency, output fragmentation and the cost of processing the whole corpus. `gpt-5.6-luna` produced no logical contradictions between fields, ran at a predictable speed of about 3 seconds per paragraph, and was competitive on cost.

**Pass 1: Semantic frame extraction.** Candidate texts passing the GBDT prefilter (`{python} f"{hd_pass1_paragraphs:,}"` unique paragraphs) are submitted to the extraction model using constrained JSON schemas enforced via `pydantic-ai`. **Traceability and audit anchors.** So that the chain can be audited end to end, every extracted frame and every disclosed activity is bound to a zero-indexed list of sentence citations inside its source paragraph (`sentence_ids`). Any aggregate index, regression coefficient or quoted case in this study can be traced back to the exact sentence published in EDGAR or spoken on the call.

### A.4 Construction of disclosure measures {.unnumbered}

Extracted semantic frames and operational activities are aggregated into six core construct measures:

$$\underbrace{\text{Semantic frames}}_{\text{Pass 1}} \Longrightarrow D, P \qquad\qquad \underbrace{\text{Disclosed AI activities}}_{\text{Pass 2}} \Longrightarrow A, G \qquad\qquad (D, A, G) \Longrightarrow S \Longrightarrow W$$

**1. AI Disclosure Intensity ($D_{it}$):** Captures the relative narrative volume of corporate AI discussion, scaled by total document length to avoid bias from verbosity:

$$D_{it} = \frac{\text{AI frames}_{it}}{\text{words}_{it} / 1{,}000}$$

**2. Communication Posture ($P_{it}$):** A seven-dimensional vector summarizing rhetorical emphasis across firm-subject claims: promotional tone ($P_{\text{prom}}$), hedging ($P_{\text{hedge}}$), risk exposure ($P_{\text{risk}}$), governance and oversight ($P_{\text{gov}}$), claim realization ($P_{\text{real}}$), customer focus ($P_{\text{cust}}$), and technical specificity ($P_{\text{spec}}$). Each dimension is measured as the proportion of the firm's AI claims exhibiting that feature.

**3. Disclosed AI Activity ($A_{it}$):** The total count of discrete operational action triples ($n_{\text{activities},it}$) across the six enterprise business domains (Operate, Sell, Build, Control, Serve, Enable).

**4. AI Activity Grounding ($G_{it}$):** An index in $[0, 1]$ measuring the proportion of five concrete evidentiary criteria met across disclosed activities: (i) identified operational business function, (ii) deployed or scaled maturity stage, (iii) named product or process, (iv) quantified performance or financial metric, and (v) named third-party technology provider.

**5. Disclosed Substance ($S_{it}$):** Grounded operational activity volume, scaling the log-transformed count of concrete activities by their average evidentiary verifiability:

$$S_{it} = \log(1 + n_{\text{activities},it}) \times G_{it}$$

**6. Decoupling ($W_{it}$):** Measures the divergence between narrative volume and verifiable operational backing:

$$W_{it} = \text{rank}(D_{it}) - \text{rank}(S_{it}) \in [-1, 1]$$

where $\text{rank}(\cdot) \in [0, 1]$ is the empirical percentile rank computed within a reporting year among AI-disclosing firms. A large positive value is a firm making strong narrative claims with little verifiable backing ("AI washing"); a negative value is a firm with substantial grounded implementation and very little promotion around it.

**Aggregation across documents.** The firm-year indicator is the **median document rate** across everything the firm published in that fiscal period. The median limits the influence of boilerplate legal exhibits, short press releases and outlier filings, which would pull an arithmetic mean around.

**Treatment of zeros and low-volume text.** A firm with no AI claims has $D_{it} = 0$, $A_{it} = 0$, $G_{it} = 0$ and $S_{it} = 0$. Decoupling ($W_{it}$) is defined only over disclosing firms ($D_{it} > 0$), since a rank gap means nothing when there is no narrative at all. For firms with only one or two claims, empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the sector-year prior is evaluated in Appendix B and the ranking does not depend on low-denominator artifacts.

### A.5 Financial data preparation, XBRL hierarchy, and market models {.unnumbered}

| Financial concept | Coverage of the firm-year panel |
|---|---:|
| Revenue | `{python} f"{fin_cov('revenue'):.0f}"`% |
| Net margin | `{python} f"{fin_cov('net_margin'):.0f}"`% |
| Capex | `{python} f"{fin_cov('capex'):.0f}"`% |
| SG&A | `{python} f"{fin_cov('sga_expense'):.0f}"`% |
| R&D expense | `{python} f"{fin_cov('rd_expense'):.0f}"`% (`{python} f"{fin_n('rd_expense'):,}"` of `{python} f"{fin_n_firmyears:,}"` firm-years; outcome only) |

: XBRL concept coverage. {#tbl-d1-xbrl-coverage}

The coverage in @tbl-d1-xbrl-coverage comes from a fallback hierarchy of alternative XBRL tags for each item: when a firm's primary tag for a concept is missing in a year, the pipeline moves to the next tag in a fixed priority order, and only then leaves the item missing. Nothing is imputed. The R&D mapping below shows that logic, including what is excluded at each step.

Disclosure dates are linked to financial fundamentals by fiscal period: an annual accounting variable matches the fiscal year of its Form 10-K, and an annual growth calculation uses a $[340, 380]$-day validity window against the nearest prior filing date. Financial ratios are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles so that a small denominator cannot distort them.

**R&D coverage and interpretation.** How R&D is reported in statutory filings varies a great deal from one industry to another. Comparable current R&D expense is built from four standardized XBRL concepts -- the primary GAAP line, its variant excluding acquired in-process cost, the dedicated software-development line, and the IFRS equivalent -- taken in that priority order. Four further lines are excluded as non-comparable: capitalized software (a balance-sheet intangible, not period expense), in-process R&D from purchase accounting (a one-time transaction charge), research tax credits (a tax benefit, not research activity) and extractive exploration expense (ASC 932). Combining the software and IFRS lines recovers 34 firm-years that narrower GAAP mappings miss, yielding `{python} f"{fin_n('rd_expense'):,}"` valid firm-years (`{python} f"{fin_cov('rd_expense'):.1f}"`% of the `{python} f"{fin_n_firmyears:,}"` total panel).

A missing R&D value comes from accounting convention in the industry, not from a failed extraction. R&D disclosure is normal in Healthcare, Technology and Manufacturing and almost absent in Financial Services, Utilities and Transportation, where the same spending is expensed inside SG&A or capitalized into physical infrastructure. Since non-reporting is decided by the business model of the industry, R&D-to-sales is never imputed as zero; doing so would treat a bank that does not report software spending as a bank with no technological innovation. In the regressions, R&D intensity is either estimated inside the disclosing subsample, with the effective sample size reported, or controlled with a non-reporting indicator.

**Market beta and estimation-window diagnostics.** For each firm-year, market beta is estimated from a one-factor market model over the 252 trading days strictly before the actual filing date of the Form 10-K. Let $R_{i,t}$ denote the daily return on the firm's adjusted close, $R_{f,t}$ the daily risk-free rate, and $(\text{MKT} - \text{RF})_t$ the daily market excess return from the Ken French Fama--French three-factor data series. The estimated regression is

$$
R_{i,t} - R_{f,t} = \alpha_i + \beta_i (\text{MKT} - \text{RF})_t + \varepsilon_{i,t}.
$$

The beta-estimation procedure identifies the first trading day on or after the filing date and takes the preceding 252 price observations. It then retains only dates for which the firm return, $(\text{MKT} - \text{RF})_t$, and $R_{f,t}$ are all available, and estimates the intercept and slope by OLS. The procedure requires at least 120 valid daily observations; otherwise beta is recorded as missing. The idiosyncratic-volatility measure uses the standard deviation of residuals from the same fitted model, annualized by $\sqrt{252}$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import pandas as pd

_mf = pd.read_parquet(gold("covariates", "firm_year", "market"))
_mf = _mf[_mf["beta_n_obs"].notna()]  # firm-years with a 10-K and a price window
mf_n_cells, mf_n_tickers = len(_mf), _mf["ticker"].nunique()
mf_year_min, mf_year_max = int(_mf["year"].min()), int(_mf["year"].max())
_beta_ok = _mf["beta"].notna()
mf_beta_n, mf_beta_pct = int(_beta_ok.sum()), 100 * _beta_ok.mean()
_win = _mf["beta_n_obs"]
mf_win_mean = _win.mean()
mf_win_median = _win.median()
mf_win_ge240_pct = 100 * (_win >= 240).mean()
mf_n_short = int((~_beta_ok).sum())
_beta = _mf.loc[_beta_ok, "beta"]
mf_beta_mean, mf_beta_median, mf_beta_sd = _beta.mean(), _beta.median(), _beta.std()
mf_beta_q1, mf_beta_q3 = _beta.quantile(0.25), _beta.quantile(0.75)
mf_beta_min, mf_beta_max = _beta.min(), _beta.max()
mf_beta_range = f"[{mf_beta_min:.2f}, {mf_beta_max:.2f}]"
```

The market-factors panel spans `{python} f"{mf_n_cells:,}"` firm-years across `{python} mf_n_tickers` tickers (`{python} mf_year_min`–`{python} mf_year_max`). Beta is available for `{python} f"{mf_beta_n:,}"` observations (`{python} f"{mf_beta_pct:.1f}"`%). The estimation window averages `{python} f"{mf_win_mean:.1f}"` return days (median `{python} f"{mf_win_median:.0f}"`), with `{python} f"{mf_win_ge240_pct:.1f}"`% using $\ge 240$ trading days. Observations with fewer than 120 trading days (`{python} mf_n_short` firm-years) are left missing rather than estimated over truncated windows. Valid betas have mean `{python} f"{mf_beta_mean:.2f}"` (median `{python} f"{mf_beta_median:.2f}"`, SD `{python} f"{mf_beta_sd:.2f}"`, IQR `{python} f"{mf_beta_q1:.2f}"`–`{python} f"{mf_beta_q3:.2f}"`, range `{python} mf_beta_range`).

### A.6 Computational environment and analytical stack {.unnumbered}

The pipeline, the feature engineering and the statistical analysis are written entirely in Python 3.12, inside an isolated and deterministic environment managed with `uv`. The stack is:

- **Data engineering:** `polars` for ingestion, text hashing and the multi-million-row Bronze and Silver Parquet transformations, and `pandas` with `NumPy` for the Gold analytical panels and the tabular aggregations.
- **NLP and embeddings:** dense representations from the Hugging Face model `BAAI/bge-m3` [@chen2024bge], which handles several languages and an 8,192-token context window, used for the semantic anchor scores.
- **Machine learning and inference:** supervised classification with `lightgbm` and `scikit-learn`; LLM extraction with `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` through Amazon Bedrock and OpenRouter, with the JSON output enforced by `pydantic-ai`.
- **Econometrics:** cross-sectional and panel regressions, fixed-effects specifications and survival diagnostics, estimated with `statsmodels` and `SciPy`.
- **Reproducibility:** all code and pipeline artifacts under Git, with deterministic seeds on every stochastic step.

### Validation protocol and inter-annotator agreement {.unnumbered}

Two of the six benchmarks in @tbl-evaluation-datasets rest on human judgment rather than LLM-to-LLM agreement: the 300-paragraph prefilter review (full-text human reading) and the 120-paragraph, 267-activity field-agreement audit. The remaining benchmarks -- the prefilter training/test set, the two out-of-domain transfer tests, and inter-judge frame agreement -- compare one LLM's output to another's (Gemini vs. Qwen), which is a consistency check, not ground truth.

### External benchmark: disclosed AI activity against AI patents {.unnumbered}

The measurement constructs are extracted from what firms write; no audited census of corporate AI deployment exists against which to check them. Prior work reaches for the same kind of external evidence: @babina2024 and @song2026 measure AI adoption through job postings and patents rather than disclosure, precisely because the text cannot be taken at face value. AI patents offer the closest external, non-textual observable of technological capacity available here. Patent publications are assigned to universe issuers via curated assignee aliases (operating subsidiaries and IP holding entities). AI patents are identified using the OECD (2025) taxonomy: five unconditional core CPC groups and 95 application groups requiring AI keywords in title or abstract.

Under statutory patent rules (35 U.S.C. § 122(b)), applications remain confidential until publication 18 months after filing. To ensure an un-truncated, stationary benchmark where all applications have matured into public documents, the comparison window closes at 2021–2023. Patents remain an incomplete benchmark: routine workflow automation rarely produces a patent. @tbl-b1-patents-controls tests whether firms disclosing more, and more grounded, AI activity hold systematically greater patented AI capacity, controlling for firm size and sector so the result is not an artifact of large firms in patent-heavy sectors disclosing more of everything.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-b1-patents-controls
#| tbl-cap: "[OLS of log(1 + AI patents, 2021-2023) on log disclosed AI activity, controlling for log market capitalization and 2-digit SIC fixed effects.]{custom-style=\"CaptionText\"}"
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

_pc = pd.read_csv(results("appendix", "patents_controls.csv")).set_index("regressor")
n_b1 = int(_pc["n"].iloc[0])
n_sic_b1 = int(_pc["n_sic"].iloc[0])
_coef_act_b1 = _pc.loc["Disclosed AI activities (log A)", "coefficient"]
_p_act_b1 = _pc.loc["Disclosed AI activities (log A)", "p"]
_coef_grd_b1 = _pc.loc["Grounded activities (log G)", "coefficient"]
_p_grd_b1 = _pc.loc["Grounded activities (log G)", "p"]

def _fmt_p(p):
    return f"{p:.1e}" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"

tbl_rows_b1 = [
    ["Disclosed AI activities ($\\log A$)", f"{_coef_act_b1:+.3f}", _fmt_p(_p_act_b1)],
    ["Grounded activities ($\\log G$)", f"{_coef_grd_b1:+.3f}", _fmt_p(_p_grd_b1)],
]
Markdown(tabulate(tbl_rows_b1, headers=["Regressor (each in a separate model with log market cap + SIC FE)", "Coefficient", "p"]))

Disclosed AI activity predicts AI patenting even after controlling for firm size and sector: with `{python} n_b1` firms across `{python} n_sic_b1` SIC groups, a one-log-point increase in disclosed AI activities is associated with `{python} f"{_coef_act_b1:.2f}"` additional log-patents (p `{python} pstr(_p_act_b1)`), and the same holds for grounded activities alone (`{python} f"{_coef_grd_b1:.2f}"`, p `{python} pstr(_p_grd_b1)`). The constructs extracted by the LLM therefore order firms in the same way as an independent measure of technological development that has nothing to do with the text.

### Error taxonomy and classification robustness {.unnumbered}

Frame extraction is deliberately non-discarding: only the prefilter gate rejects a passage outright, and it is calibrated to keep the false-negative rate low (recall $\ge 0.92$) at the cost of passing some borderline material forward. Passages that reach the extractor but yield no semantic frame are the visible trace of that trade-off -- most commonly passages containing only incidental keywords, macro commentary, or generic disclaimers that the gate's high-recall calibration cannot rule out on lexical features alone. Because the extractor, not the gate, makes the final call on these cases, no relevant disclosure is dropped silently before an LLM has read it in context.

Among the frames that are extracted, the discrepancies concentrate at one margin: between a forward-looking promotional claim and a description of early exploratory research. These borderline cases show no systematic correlation with firm size, leverage or sector. Collapsing the borderline categories, or reweighting them, leaves the firm-level posture scores and the archetype assignments essentially unchanged (Spearman $\rho > 0.96$ in every specification tried), so the empirical findings do not depend on the residual measurement noise.

### Aggregation reliability and empirical-Bayes shrinkage {.unnumbered}

Firm-year rates aggregate from document-level frame counts through the median. Two checks test how much that choice matters. First, log-transforming the concept counts before aggregation gives higher year-over-year reliability than aggregating raw shares ($\rho = 0.845$ against $0.528$), so the log transform adds stability on top of what the median already provides. Second, when a firm has very little AI-related text, and a firm-year rate therefore rests on a handful of documents, the rate is shrunk toward the sample mean by empirical-Bayes estimation [@efron1973], which lowers the variance of an estimate built on thin evidence without throwing any document away.

## Appendix C: Supplementary Disclosure and AI Activity Results {.unnumbered}

### Archetypal Analysis: formal specification {.unnumbered}

Archetypal Analysis [@cutler1994] represents every firm $i$ as a convex combination of $k$ extreme boundary vertices in the standardized seven-dimensional posture space:

$$x_i \approx \sum_{j=1}^k w_{ij} z_j, \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{j=1}^k w_{ij} = 1, \quad w_{ij} \ge 0$$

where $z_j \in \mathbb{R}^7$ are the archetypal coordinate vectors and $w_{ij}$ are the barycentric weights reflecting firm $i$'s posture portfolio.

The archetype count ($k=3$) used throughout this thesis is chosen by the `{python} hd_boot_reps`-replicate dual bootstrap reported in Chapter 2 (@fig-archetype-stability). The supporting robustness checks follow: a principal-components diagnostic, the substantive comparison against $k=2$, a fixed-$N$ check, a K-means cross-check and out-of-sample temporal validation.

### Archetype count: PCA, $k=2$ comparison, fixed-$N$, and K-means robustness {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# k=2 Archetypal Analysis fit (same population, same 8 posture dimensions,
# same seed as the k=3 fit in Chapter 2), read from
# scripts/analytics/posture/archetype_k2_fit.py's output rather than fit
# inline, purely to source the substantive-rejection paragraph below from

k2_promo = _k2["k2_promo"]
k2_risk = _k2["k2_risk"]
k2_gov = _k2["k2_gov"]
k2_spec = _k2["k2_spec"]
```

**Why $k = 2$ is rejected on substantive grounds.** Two poles are mathematically stable under both bootstrap regimes, but they remove governance orientation altogether and with it the institutional difference between board oversight and a statutory risk warning. At $k = 2$, Archetype 0 has promotional $=$ `{python} f"{k2_promo[0]:+.2f}"`, risk $=$ `{python} f"{k2_risk[0]:+.2f}"`, governance $=$ `{python} f"{k2_gov[0]:+.2f}"`, specificity $=$ `{python} f"{k2_spec[0]:+.2f}"`; Archetype 1 has promotional $=$ `{python} f"{k2_promo[1]:+.2f}"`, risk $=$ `{python} f"{k2_risk[1]:+.2f}"`, governance $=$ `{python} f"{k2_gov[1]:+.2f}"`, specificity $=$ `{python} f"{k2_spec[1]:+.2f}"`. A discrete K-means benchmark on the same standardized posture matrix reproduces the same three-archetype partition.

A principal components diagnostic confirms that the space cannot be collapsed into one score without heavy information loss: the first two components capture `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[0] + hd_pca_ev[1]:.1f}"`% of the variance (PC1: `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[0]:.1f}"`%, PC2: `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[1]:.1f}"`%).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-a2-six-dimensions

from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

dist = _apj["distributions"]
func = _apj["function_families"]

def col(items):
    # Raw identifiers (e.g. "infrastructure_investment") have no space for Word
    # to wrap on in a narrow column, so a long one gets hyphenated mid-word;
    # replacing underscores with spaces gives it a break point.
    return [[k.replace("_", " "), f"{v:.1f}%"] for k, v in sorted(items.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])]

def side_by_side(pairs):
    cols = [col(items) for _, items in pairs]
    n = max(len(c) for c in cols)
    rows = []
    for i in range(n):
        row = []
        for c in cols:
            row.extend(c[i] if i < len(c) else ["", ""])
        rows.append(row)
    headers = []
    for label, _ in pairs:
        headers += [label, "%"]
    return tabulate(rows, headers=headers)

t1 = side_by_side([("Action", dist["action"]), ("Maturity stage", dist["stage"]), ("Target audience", dist["target"])])
t2 = side_by_side([("AI source", dist["source"]), ("Evidence strength", dist["evidence_type"]), ("Business function", func)])
Markdown(t1 + "\n\n" + t2)
```

*Notes:* Computed from the firm-level activity-profile summary. "Business function" has no single dominant category comparable to `customer_service` for customer-success work specifically. Customer success (retention/expansion) is not coded as a separate family from customer support in the current taxonomy.
:::

### Disclosed activity counts conditioned on disclosure volume {.unnumbered}

Frames and activities come from the same corporate text, so the difference in disclosed activity across archetypes could simply reflect that some firms write more. Disclosed AI activity counts are therefore regressed on the archetypes, controlling for total AI disclosure volume ($\log(1 + \text{AI frames})$), in a negative binomial regression:

$$
\log \mathbb{E}[\text{AI Activities}_i] = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{VocalSubstantives}_i + \beta_2 \text{GovernanceLed}_i + \gamma \log(1 + \text{Frames}_i)
$$

```{python}
#| label: tbl-4-1b-volume-adjusted
#| tbl-cap: "[Disclosed AI activity count by archetype, before and after conditioning on total AI disclosure volume.]{custom-style=\"CaptionText\"}"
#| echo: false

from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown


reg = _var  # results/posture/strategy_dimensions_diagnostics.json["activity_volume_regression"], loaded above
OTHERS = ["Governance-Led Disclosers", "Vocal Substantives"]

def fmt_p(p):
    return "<0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"

def fmt_ci(spec, a):
    lo, hi = reg[spec][a]["ratio_ci95"]
    return f"[{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]"

rows = [[a, f"{reg['raw'][a]['ratio']:.2f}x", fmt_ci("raw", a), fmt_p(reg['raw'][a]['p']),
        f"{reg['volume_adjusted'][a]['ratio']:.2f}x", fmt_ci("volume_adjusted", a), fmt_p(reg['volume_adjusted'][a]['p'])]
        for a in OTHERS]
rows.append(["log(1 + AI frames)", "-", "-", "-", f"{reg['log_frames_coef']:+.2f} (coef.)", "-", fmt_p(reg['log_frames_p'])])
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=[f"Archetype vs. {reg['reference']}", "Raw ratio", "95% CI", "p",
                                  "Volume-adj. ratio", "95% CI", "p"]))
```

::: {custom-style="FigureNote"}
*Notes:* Volume control is log frame count. Reference category: Defensive Disclosers.
:::

A statistically significant difference survives the volume control (@tbl-4-1b-volume-adjusted). At identical narrative volume, Vocal Substantives still report `{python} f"{hd_vs_ratio:.2f}"` times as many operational AI activities as Defensive Disclosers ($p$ `{python} pstr(_var["volume_adjusted"]["Vocal Substantives"]["p"])`), while Governance-Led Disclosers report `{python} f"{hd_gl_ratio:.2f}"` times as many ($p$ `{python} pstr(_var["volume_adjusted"]["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["p"])`). Total disclosure volume does explain a large share of the raw variation, since the log frame count alone gives a pseudo-$R^2$ of `{python} f"{hd_vol_r2:.2f}"`, but posture is still not the same thing as verbosity: it corresponds to different rates of disclosed technological deployment.

### External AI technology ecosystem {.unnumbered}

The lexicon behind this measure lives in `configs/ai_vendor_ecosystems.yaml`: one entry per provider family, with the ecosystem it belongs to, its specific country and its role in the AI stack. Three rules govern what counts. Country and demonym words are absent by construction, so a paragraph discussing the Chinese market without naming a Chinese provider contributes nothing. Ambiguous names -- ordinary words, personal names, multi-vendor products -- are admitted only with a corroborating term in the same paragraph, so "copilot" needs Microsoft or GitHub, "arm" needs an Arm-qualified term, and "claude" needs Anthropic or a model name. And a filer naming its own products is excluded, since the measure is the reach of external suppliers rather than the reach of a firm's own brand. Presence is recorded once per document, so repetition cannot inflate a supplier's reach, and ecosystems overlap: a document naming both NVIDIA and DeepSeek counts for the United States and for China.

Every provider family named by at least one S&P 500 firm inside its AI disclosure appears in @tbl-c3-vendor-ecosystem, with the literal names it was matched on. The fifteen most-cited families carry the concentration shown in @fig-vendor-providers; the remainder shows how thin the tail is, and how little of it sits outside the United States.

```{python}

## Appendix D: Supplementary Robustness and Alternative Specifications {.unnumbered}

### Break-date sweep for the December 2023 warning {.unnumbered}

The acceleration in risk and governance framing predates the regulator. The step estimated at December 2023 is indistinguishable from zero in both series ($p$ `{python} pstr(_at("Risk frames", _sec_break, "p_step"))` for risk framing and $p$ `{python} pstr(_at("Governance frames", _sec_break, "p_step"))` for governance framing), and refitting the same specification at every candidate break month from January 2023 to June 2025 fits best in `{python} _best_break("Risk frames")` and `{python} _best_break("Governance frames")` respectively -- three quarters or more before the warning -- with the estimated slope change shrinking the later the break is placed (@tbl-e-break-dates). The reported months are the best-fitting break of each series, the warning itself, and the range either side of it.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-e-break-dates
#| tbl-cap: "[Interrupted time series of risk and governance framing, refitted at alternative break dates.]{custom-style=\"CaptionText\"}"
#| echo: false
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

_shown = ["2023-01", "2023-03", "2023-06", "2023-12", "2024-06", "2024-12", "2025-06"]
_rows = []
for outcome in ["Risk frames", "Governance frames"]:
    best = _best_break(outcome)
    for month in _shown:
        mark = " (best fit)" if month == best else (" (SEC warning)" if month == _sec_break else "")
        _rows.append([outcome if month == _shown[0] else "", month + mark,
                      f"{_at(outcome, month, 'step'):+.4f}", pstr(_at(outcome, month, "p_step")),
                      f"{_at(outcome, month, 'slope_change'):+.4f}", pstr(_at(outcome, month, "p_slope_change")),
                      f"{_at(outcome, month, 'r2'):.3f}"])
Markdown(tabulate(_rows, headers=["Series", "Break date", "Step", "p", "Slope change", "p", "$R^2$"]))
```

::: {custom-style="FigureNote"}
*Notes:* Monthly series per 1,000 words over every document published in the month, from January 2021, with quarter-of-year seasonality and the log number of reporting firms held constant and Newey-West standard errors at six lags. "Step" is the immediate level change at the break, "slope change" the change in monthly trend afterwards. A break at one date cannot be separated from anything else happening at that date: the sweep says which month the series turns, not what turned it.
:::

### Archetype recovery under a Form 10-K-only refit {.unnumbered}

@tbl-e-10k-refit recomputes the archetypal weights ($w_{\text{Vocal}}, w_{\text{Gov}}, w_{\text{Def}}$) on Form 10-K frames alone and correlates them firm by firm with the full-corpus weights. ### Decoupling index construction and sensitivity {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import pandas as pd

_wv = results_json("washing", "washing_score_validation.json")
w_n_panel, w_n_firms = _wv["n_panel"], _wv["n_firms"]
w_n_firmyears_total = len(pd.read_parquet(gold("spines", "firm_year", "firm_year")))
w_n_firms_total = len(pd.read_parquet(gold("spines", "firm", "firm")))
```

**Decoupling index ($W$), full specification.** Disclosed substance is defined as:
$$
\text{Substance}_{it} = \log(1 + n_{\text{activities},it}) \times \text{Grounding}_{it}
$$
where $\text{Grounding}_{it}$ averages five empirical-Bayes shrunk concreteness markers across disclosed AI activities (named function, deployed/scaled stage, named product or process, quantified outcome, named provider). The index is computed as:
$$
W_{it} = \text{pctrank}(\text{Disclosure}_{it}) - \text{pctrank}(\text{Substance}_{it})
$$
where $\text{Disclosure}_{it}$ is AI frames per 1,000 words. Both percentile ranks are calculated within the disclosing sample ($\text{Disclosure}_{it} > 0$: `{python} w_n_panel` of `{python} w_n_firmyears_total` firm-years, `{python} w_n_firms` of `{python} w_n_firms_total` firms pooled 2021–2026). $W$ is non-parametric: it requires no regression, fixed effects, or fitted residuals.

**Percentile ranking versus z-score standardization.** Percentile ranks are used instead of z-scores. $\text{Disclosure}_{it}$ has a much heavier right tail than $\text{Substance}_{it}$ (a maximum $z$ of 18.5 against 4.3), and under z-scores the firms with the largest volume of grounded activity, Microsoft or NVIDIA for example, end up in the washing tail as soon as their narrative volume is an even bigger outlier than their substance.

The Spearman correlation between the z-score and the percentile version is 0.723, and the two share only 43 of 102 firm-years in the top-5% tail (Jaccard = 0.267). With percentile ranking, the tail contains what it should contain: firms with a lot of narrative and very little grounded activity behind it.

**Substance functional form.** An additive form, $z(\log(1+n_{\text{activities}})) + z(\text{Grounding})$, and a grounded-count form, $\log(1 + n_{\text{activities}} \times \text{Grounding})$, yield near-identical rankings to the multiplicative baseline. Substance under the multiplicative and grounded-count forms correlates at Spearman $\rho = 0.991$ ($n = `{python} w_n_panel`$), producing decoupling indices with $\rho = 0.986$ and 89 of 102 shared top-tail firm-years (Jaccard = 0.774). The multiplicative form is preferred because it penalizes ungrounded volume: a firm with many vague activities does not automatically outscore one with fewer, well-grounded actions.

**Residual decoupling index ($W^*$, a Jones-model analogue).** To check that subtracting ranks does not create an artifact that a parametric residualization would avoid, an earnings-management style regression [@jones1991] predicts the substance rank from the disclosure rank, controlling for firm scale and two-digit SIC industry fixed effects:
$$
\text{pctrank}(\text{Substance}_{it}) = \alpha_s + \beta_1 \text{pctrank}(\text{Disclosure}_{it}) + \beta_2 \log(\text{MarketCap}_{it}) + \varepsilon_{it}
$$
The residual decoupling measure is defined as $W^*_{it} \equiv -\hat{\varepsilon}_{it}$, such that positive values denote firms whose grounded operational substance falls short of what is expected given their narrative volume, scale, and sector. $W^*$ exhibits a Spearman rank correlation of $\rho = 0.808$ ($p < 0.0001$, $n = 1,664$) with non-parametric $W$, and shares $61.9\%$ of firm-years in the extreme top-5% decoupling tail ($52$ of $84$). The rank-based measure $W$ therefore captures the same economic decoupling as a fully residualized parametric index, and it does so without distributional assumptions and without the instability that a small industry cell would bring.

**Persistence and within-year reliability.** Decoupling is a lasting communication posture rather than annual reporting noise. Across `{python} persistence_n_pairs` consecutive firm-year pairs the year-over-year Spearman $\rho =$ `{python} f"{persistence_rho:+.3f}"` (p `{python} persistence_p_str`), and a split-half check within a single year -- $W$ computed on two random halves of each firm-year's documents -- reproduces the same ordering, $\rho =$ `{python} f"{split_half_rho:+.3f}"` (p `{python} split_half_p_str`, $n =$ `{python} f"{split_half_n:,}"`), so the measure is not an artifact of which documents happen to fall in a given year. @tbl-c4-washing-validation summarizes both alongside the rest of the validation battery.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-c4-washing-validation
#| tbl-cap: "[Decoupling index ($W$) validation summary (firm-year panel, firm-years disclosing AI).]{custom-style=\"CaptionText\"}"
#| echo: false
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

d = _wv

def fmt_p(p):
    return "<0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"

mc = d["mechanical_consistency_vs_grounding"]
pers = d["persistence"]
sh = d["split_half"]
rows = [
    ["Construct consistency vs. Grounding", f"n={mc['n']}", f"{mc['spearman']:+.3f}", fmt_p(mc['p'])],
    ["Persistence (W_t vs. W_t+1)", f"n={pers['n_pairs']} pairs", f"{pers['spearman']:+.3f}", fmt_p(pers['p'])],
    ["Split-half (years split per firm)", f"n={sh['n']} firms", f"{sh['spearman']:+.3f}", fmt_p(sh['p'])],
]
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=["Check", "Sample", "Spearman", "p"]))
```

::: {custom-style="FigureNote"}
*Notes:* Construct consistency against Grounding is restricted to firm-years with at least one disclosed AI activity ($n = `{python} mc['n']`$). Because Grounding is an internal component of Substance, this confirms mechanical consistency rather than independent validity. The economic-coherence tests show that $W$ tracks R&D intensity negatively without tracking firm size, valuation, or risk.
:::

@tbl-call-beta-paper evaluates the baseline post-call beta model (window $[+21,+63]$) against accounting controls (ROA and leverage) on the same window, and against four further checks estimated directly from raw daily prices over the $[+21,+126]$ window: the Fama–French 3-factor benchmark, a full-year post-call window (+252 days), within-firm fixed effects, and first differences (Delta Beta).

## Appendix E: SEC Comment-Letter Inventory and Case Comparisons {.unnumbered}

This appendix documents the search for SEC staff comment letters that touch corporate AI disclosure, the classification of every letter found, and the case comparisons reported in the regulatory-scrutiny analysis.

### Search and classification {.unnumbered}

The EDGAR full-text index was searched for staff comment letters (form `UPLOAD`) and issuer responses (`CORRESP`) filed between 2022-01-01 and `{python} sec_cases["search_window"].split("..")[1]`. Search terms included "artificial intelligence", "AI", "machine learning", "generative", "large language", and hyphenated compounds ("AI-driven", "AI-powered", "AI-enabled"). Queries were restricted to the `{python} hd_n_universe` universe issuers, and every matching letter was read in full.

Correspondence for eight universe issuers matched at least one term, plus Match Group, which joined after the panel date (@tbl-g1-sec-letters). Reading the letters in full shows that most of those matches have nothing to do with AI disclosure. Two responses, from Apple and Amazon, matched only because of a confidential-treatment page code ("AI-001") or an incidental reference inside a climate-risk review, and they are omitted.

### Matched-peer comparison for the direct and adjacent cases {.unnumbered}

For each case, annual reports are indexed in event time $k$, where $k = 0$ denotes the first Form 10-K filed post-letter and $k = -1$ the final pre-letter filing. Three control peers within the same two-digit SIC industry are selected via Mahalanobis nearest-neighbour matching on pre-letter log market capitalization, AI claim density, promotional density, and pre-letter claim trend ($\Delta k_{-2 \to -1}$). Control 10-Ks are aligned by filing year. With one direct and one adjacent case, @tbl-g2-sec-cases reports raw case comparisons without regression estimation.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-g2-sec-cases
#| tbl-cap: "[Annual-report AI disclosure measures around the SEC letter: treated firm versus the mean of three matched industry peers.]{custom-style=\"CaptionText\"}"
#| echo: false
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown
_LAB = {"claim_density": "AI claim density (per 1k words)", "realized_density": "Realized-integration claims (per 1k words)",
        "quant_density": "Quantified-metric claims (per 1k words)", "specificity_index": "Specificity index (per frame)", "w": "Decoupling ($W$)"}
_KS = [-2, -1, 0, 1]
_rows = []
for t, c in sec_cases["cases"].items():
    pos = {k: i for i, k in enumerate(c["k"])}
    _rows.append([f"**{t}**", "Filing year of the 10-K"] + [str(c["year"][pos[k]]) if k in pos else "—" for k in _KS])
    for m, lab in _LAB.items():
        cells = []
        for k in _KS:
            if k not in pos:
                cells.append("—"); continue
            a, b = c["treated"][m][pos[k]], c["controls_mean"][m][pos[k]]
            cells.append(f"{'—' if a is None else f'{a:.3f}'} / {'—' if b is None else f'{b:.3f}'}")
        _rows.append([t, lab] + cells)
_hdr = ["Case", "Measure (treated / peers)"] + [f"k = {k:+d}" if k else "k = 0" for k in _KS]
Markdown(tabulate(_rows, headers=_hdr))
```

::: {custom-style="FigureNote"}
*Notes:* Welltower's letter (2025-04-28) reviews the FY2024 10-K filed in February 2025 ($k=-1$); the first post-letter annual report is the FY2025 10-K filed in February 2026 ($k=0$), so no $k=+1$ observation exists yet. Arista's letters (2024-07-25 and 2024-10-16) review the FY2023 10-K; $k=0$ is the FY2024 10-K filed in February 2025. ## Appendix F: Sector, Cohort, and Rollup Disaggregation {.unnumbered}

The disclosure-posture, activity, decoupling, and credibility results above are computed on the pooled S&P 500 panel. This appendix disaggregates those constructs by two-digit SIC sector, filer cohort, and rollup method, using the same firm-year and activity-level tables read elsewhere in this thesis; no new constructs are introduced.

### Is the grounding decline within firms, or driven by new filers? {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-h5-cohort-grounding
#| tbl-cap: "[Mean AI activity grounding ($G$) by year, fixed cohort vs. new filers.]{custom-style=\"CaptionText\"}"
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

tbl = pd.read_csv(results("washing", "appendix_g_cohort_grounding.csv")).set_index("year")
y0 = int(tbl.index.min())
years = sorted(tbl.index)
rows = [[y, f"{tbl.loc[y, 'fixed_cohort_grounding']:.3f}" if pd.notna(tbl.loc[y, "fixed_cohort_grounding"]) else "—",
         f"{tbl.loc[y, 'new_filer_year_grounding']:.3f}" if pd.notna(tbl.loc[y, "new_filer_year_grounding"]) else "—"]
        for y in years]
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=["Year", f"Fixed cohort ({y0} filers), $G$", "New filers' first year, $G$"]))
```

::: {custom-style="FigureNote"}
*Notes:* Fixed cohort: firms present since the first panel year. New filers: firms in their first disclosing year.
:::

Grounding falls inside the same fixed cohort of firms, so the decline is not only a composition effect from less-grounded firms entering the panel. Firms that have been disclosing AI activity since the first panel year show grounding falling over the whole period, and each year's new filers enter at or below that year's incumbent level, never above it. Both mechanisms are at work: existing disclosers dilute their own claims over time, and new entrants arrive already diluted.

### Do the results depend on the rollup method? {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-h8-rollup-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "[Share of disclosed AI activities meeting the named-product-or-metric grounding bar, by channel, under two rollup methods.]{custom-style=\"CaptionText\"}"
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

tbl = pd.read_csv(results("washing", "appendix_g_rollup_sensitivity.csv")).set_index("channel")
tbl = tbl.rename(columns={"activity_weighted_pct": "Activity-weighted (pooled)", "firm_weighted_pct": "Firm-weighted (equal per firm)"})
rows = [[ch] + [f"{tbl.loc[ch, c]:.1f}%" for c in tbl.columns] for ch in tbl.index]
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=["Channel"] + list(tbl.columns)))
```

Activity-weighted rollups (each disclosed activity counted once, so heavy disclosers dominate) and firm-weighted rollups (each firm-year counted once regardless of how many activities it discloses) answer different questions: "how grounded is the typical disclosed activity?" versus "how grounded is the typical firm's disclosure?" They give different levels here: the firm-weighted grounded share runs roughly `{python} f"{(tbl['Activity-weighted (pooled)'] - tbl['Firm-weighted (equal per firm)']).min():.0f}"`–`{python} f"{(tbl['Activity-weighted (pooled)'] - tbl['Firm-weighted (equal per firm)']).max():.0f}"` percentage points below the activity-weighted share in both channels, because firms with fewer disclosed activities tend to ground a smaller share of them.

Both rollups agree on the qualitative finding that motivates the credibility chapter: calls are more grounded than filings under either weighting.

# AI Statement {.unnumbered}

Generative AI served two roles in this thesis. Both are declared here under program rules.

First, large language models served as measurement tools. A zero-shot LLM extractor (gpt-5.6-luna) extracted semantic frames from candidate paragraphs. It was accessed via an API with schema-constrained outputs. The same model extracted the inventory of disclosed AI activities. 

The models did not produce empirical results directly. Both acted as annotators running a fixed, documented prompt. I checked their outputs against two human-audited samples (300 paragraphs for the prefilter, 120 paragraphs / 267 activities for extracted activity fields). I also checked cross-model agreement. Deterministic code then computed every downstream construct from these structured outputs.

Second, LLMs (Anthropic Claude, via Claude Code; and Google Gemini, via Antigravity CLI) served as tools while preparing this work. They helped write and debug both pipeline and analytics scripts. They helped draft figures and tables from computed data. They also helped check references, find source PDFs, and both spellcheck and iterate on drafts. All research questions, hypotheses, design choices, interpretations, and conclusions are the author's own. Every number reported comes from the author's code on the author's data. The author takes full responsibility for all the content.
